presets.title: Aman rice then winter potato rotation
presets.summary: Hybrid Aman in the monsoon followed by potato in the cool dry season fits the Rangpur calendar and the listed Aman-potato rotations. It is not a safe unconditional plan on this 0.09 ha field because potato needs reliable dry-season irrigation, which is only limited here, and hybrid Aman needs fresh seed and inputs every year. With assured irrigation for potato and good drainage for Aman, the rotation is workable.
reasons: Aman rice is the monsoon crop and potato is a cool dry-season crop, so they do not clash in the same season on the same field.
Research for Rangpur lists Aman to potato rotations, including potato-based patterns with T. Aman, supporting this sequence in principle.
Clay loam at pH about 6 is generally suitable for both rice and potato in Bangladesh, based on general agronomy knowledge.
The long fallow from March to May avoids trying to grow a dry-season crop without water, but wastes land that a short mungbean crop could use.
risks: Limited irrigation may be insufficient for potato from December to February, causing poor tuber bulking and low yield.
Hybrid Aman seed loses hybrid vigour if saved, so seed must be bought fresh each year, raising cost and supply risk.
Late Aman harvest can delay potato sowing, and early monsoon waterlogging can damage Aman on low-lying clay loam.
Potato disease and rice blast pressure increase if the same field is cropped intensively without rotation diversity or clean seed.
requirements: Assured irrigation for potato in December to February, with a backup source if the limited supply fails.
Fresh hybrid Aman seed each season, plus fertilizer and plant protection as advised for Rangpur by local extension.
Good field drainage and timely Aman harvest in November so potato can be sown in December.
Do not save hybrid Aman seed for the next crop.

Aman rice followed by mustard as a lower-water winter crop than potato

risks: Limited irrigation is the main risk: potato in the dry season needs regular water, and failure at tuber initiation or bulking will cut yield sharply.
Late Aman harvest or monsoon flooding delaying land preparation can push potato sowing late into cold or pre-monsoon heat.
Potato disease in humid conditions and rice disease/pests in monsoon can cause losses without timely management and clean seed.
Hybrid Aman seed cost and need for fresh seed each season strain a medium budget on 0.08 ha.
requirements: Confirm a reliable irrigation source for potato from November to February before sowing, with ability to irrigate at critical stages.
Sow Aman in June and harvest by late October so potato can be sown in November; use a short-duration Aman variety if harvest is late.
Use certified seed potato and hybrid Aman seed, and follow Fertilizer Recommendation Guide 2024 rates for Rangpur rather than guessing doses.
Ensure drainage after Aman harvest so the field is not waterlogged for potato planting.
alternatives: Aman rice followed by mustard, which needs less irrigation than potato in the dry season
Short Aman rice followed by potato followed by mungbean, a research-backed Rangpur rotation

presets.dropLine: Drop the potato part if you cannot guarantee irrigation in November to February, because dry-season potato will fail without water.

suggestions.line: Mustard uses less dry-season water than potato and fits the Aman to dry-season rotation on limited irrigation.
Research-backed Rangpur rotation that adds short mungbean after potato to use residual moisture and improve soil.

presets.title: Potato then mungbean, monsoon fallow
presets.summary: Potato in the cool dry winter followed by short mungbean in the hot pre-monsoon fits Rangpur seasons and avoids monsoon waterlogging by leaving the field fallow Jun-Oct. It can work on this small clay-loam field, but potato needs assured dry-season water, so limited irrigation is the main constraint.
reasons: Potato suits the cool dry Nov-Feb season in Rangpur and mungbean is a short 55-58 day crop that can be sown after potato harvest in Mar and harvested before monsoon, a pattern tested in Rangpur potato-based systems.
Leaving Jun-Oct fallow avoids growing either crop in the hot wet monsoon when low-lying Tista Meander fields can flood or waterlog.
Soil pH ~6 clay loam is generally workable for both crops with drainage, as general Bangladesh agronomy guidance notes, but clay loam needs timely drainage for potato tubers.
risks: Limited irrigation may be insufficient for potato, which needs regular water through the dry winter; water stress will cut tuber yield.
Late potato harvest delays mungbean sowing and pushes it into hotter, drier conditions and monsoon onset risk.
Potato disease and mungbean pest pressure increase if seed quality is poor or crops are grown repeatedly without rotation diversity.
requirements: Confirm assured irrigation for potato from Nov to Feb before committing the full 0.08 ha; reduce potato area if water is not assured.
Sow potato in early-mid Nov and harvest by late Feb, then sow mungbean immediately in early Mar to finish before monsoon.
Use healthy seed potato and quality mungbean seed, ensure field drainage, and do not sow either crop in Jun-Oct flood period.
alternatives: Use the monsoon for Aman rice instead of fallow if drainage and seed are available, as in the researched Short Aman to potato to mungbean pa

evidence.title: Improvement of potato based cropping patterns by inclusion of short duration mungbean and T. Aman rice in Monga prone areas of Rangpur

suggestions.line: Uses the monsoon for Aman and winter for potato, fitting this floodplain field better than a monsoon fallow.
Both fit the cool dry winter season and need less monsoon exposure, but still require dry-season water.

presets.title: Aman rice then Mustard rotation
presets.summary: Hybrid Aman in the monsoon followed by Mustard in the cool dry season fits the Rangpur climate and the listed Aman-Mustard rotations. It can work on this clay loam field, but Mustard in the dry season needs timely limited irrigation and Aman needs good monsoon water and drainage. With those inputs secured, this two-crop rotation is reasonable.
reasons: Aman rice duration of 135 days fits the Jun-Oct monsoon season in Rangpur, and Mustard duration of 75-80 days fits sowing in Nov and harvesting in Feb in the cool dry season.
Research rotations for this area include Aman followed by Mustard, showing the sequence is agronomically recognised in north-west Bangladesh.
Clay loam at pH ~6 is generally suitable for both rice and mustard in Bangladesh (general agronomy knowledge).
Aman relies mainly on monsoon rain, so limited irrigation is less critical for Aman than for the dry-season Mustard crop.
risks: Low-lying Tista Meander fields can flood or waterlog in monsoon, damaging Aman if drainage is poor.
Mustard in Nov-Feb will suffer in a dry spell if the limited irrigation cannot provide water at flowering and pod filling.
Hybrid Aman seed must be bought fresh each year and costs more than inbred seed, which matters on a medium budget and 0.08 ha.
Mustard is vulnerable to aphids and diseases in cool humid weather, and Aman to blast and other rice diseases in wet weather.
requirements: Secure at least 1-2 timely irrigations for Mustard in Dec-Jan, or a reliable residual moisture plan, before committing the full 0.08 ha.
Use fresh hybrid Aman seed each season and ensure nursery and transplanting labour for Jun-Jul.
Ensure field drainage and bunds to reduce monsoon waterlogging, and harvest Aman by late Oct so Mustard can be sown in Nov.
Follow Fertilizer Recommendation Guide rates for soil pH ~6 clay loam rather than guessing doses.
alternatives: Aman rice followed by Potato in winter, if irrigation for potato is more reliable than for mustard
Short Aman rice followed by Mungbean in spring, to use residual moisture and reduce dry-season irrigation need

suggestions.line: Potato is a listed Aman rotation in Rangpur and suits the cool dry season if irrigation is available.
Short Aman to potato to mungbean is a listed rotation; mungbean in spring needs less dry-season water than mustard.

presets.title: Mango orchard only on raised, well-drained ground
presets.summary: Mango can grow in Rangpur in general, but this Tista Meander Floodplain field is low-lying and can flood or waterlog in the monsoon, which mango trees tolerate poorly. On 0.08 ha it is also a long-wait perennial with no income for several years and needs dry-season water while young. It is only reasonable if the exact plot is raised and drains quickly after rain.
reasons: Mango is a common fruit tree in Bangladesh and pH ~6 clay loam is not by itself a barrier (general agronomy knowledge).
The field is in a low-lying floodplain where monsoon waterlogging is a stated risk, and mango roots are damaged by prolonged standing water.
Limited irrigation is a problem for establishment in the hot, dry pre-monsoon period, even though mature trees need less water.
At 0.08 ha, wide mango spacing means very few trees and several years before meaningful harvest, so it cannot be the sole income plan for most smallholders.
risks: Monsoon flooding or waterlogging causing root rot and tree death
Dry-season water stress for young grafted trees under limited irrigation
Long delay to first income and vulnerability to pests and diseases over a perennial life
Loss of the whole field to one flood event because a single perennial crop occupies all the land
requirements: Plant only on the highest, raised part of the plot that does not stay flooded or waterlogged in monsoon, with a drainage ditch
Use grafted, disease-free mango saplings of a locally recommended variety and plant at the start of the rains on raised pits
Provide watering through the first 2-3 dry seasons, mulch, and staking, and budget for pest and disease management
Do not convert the entire 0.08 ha to mango if the farmer needs annual income; keep part for annual crops or add a faster secondary fruit
alternatives: Mango with guava on raised ground
Guava with lemon on raised ground
Mango with annual intercrops in the first years
presets.dropLine: Drop the mango-only orchard if this plot stays flooded or waterlogged for days in the monsoon, because the trees will likely die.

suggestions.line: Guava bears earlier than mango and tolerates wetter conditions better, spreading risk on this small floodplain plot.
Both are faster-bearing secondary fruits than mango alone and suit a small raised homestead orchard.
